newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico privatizations seen likely to proceed.
newsitem.headline: Mexico privatizations seen likely to proceed.

text.p: Mexican privatizations are likely to proceed, albeit sluggishly, despite setbacks to the ruling party in this week's elections. analysts said.

Petrochemicals, ports, railroads -- all sell-offs that could stick in the craw of a belligerent Congress -- were approved in the last legislature dominated by President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
That means reversing them would be hard, despite a surge from the opposition in the mid-term vote, the analysts said.
"Of all the reforms (President Ernesto) Zedillo has set himself up to do, I would say very little would get stuck," Alfredo Thorne, J.P. Morgan economist in Mexico, told Reuters.
"Most of the privatizations have already been approved, even secondary petrochemicals."
With three years left of the Zedillo administration, the government says the bulk of that time will be spent wrapping up existing privatization projects, not embarking on new ones.

"Right now, the biggest challenge is to complete the work. We want to finalize the railroads, we have to start with the airports and complete the ports," Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner told Reuters Financial Television.
"And we have to start with the petrochemicals, which I think is a big package to fulfill probably in the next 12 to 18 months."

Some businessmen believe that is not ambitious enough. In the industrial heartland of Monterrey recently, Luis Sada, head of the local Mexican Employers Confederation and president of the Mexican subsidiary of Deere and Co, said in an interview that no state industry should be considered too sacred to sell.
"Neither the Federal Electricity Commission, nor Pemex," he said, referring to the symbol of Mexican sovereign, oil monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos. "Everything must be privatized."

Such free-market advocates argue that Mexico has to take a slash-and-burn approach on deregulation to get to double-digit growth rates that it has not achieved for decades, and to shed its still-cumbersome debt burden. They firmly believe that is where Mexico should be headed.
The only roadblock is politics.
Just putting the outdated and smog-belching secondary petrochemical plants on the market cost Zedillo dearly, and it was his own PRI that stood in the way.

Its legislators forced him last year to row back on the full privatization that he had sought, putting a 49 percent limit on private investment on existing plants. The petrochemical industry was furious, but politics prevailed.

With Congress now stuffed with more legislators from the opposition, and the PRI probably robbed of its 68-year majority after Sunday's vote, analysts believe getting too ambitious on future privatization would be a recipe for gridlock.
"It's not going to be so easy to initiate new reforms, but on the existing ones I don't see any complications in the immediate future," said Carlos Rosales, economist at Bancomer.

J.P. Morgan's Thorne noted that Zedillo can leave open a way to sidestep politically risky privatizations, by giving private investors concessions to build their own electricity or petrochemical plants.
"If he's very clever, he will tell them 'Go ahead, if you want cheaper electricity build the plants yourself. We will put it into the grid'."

The president also has a means of calming left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which made the largest gains in Congress in Sunday's vote and has traditionally been most stubborn in resisting Zedillo's reforms.
Analysts say he could give into its calls for an increase in social spending in exchange for its support on reforms.
It would be an alliance of unlikely bedfellows, but Thorne believes the PRD is a "new populist" party, not the radical left of old. There may be room for a meeting ground.
"It's not like a Communist party negotiating with the far right," he said.
